section.title: Longing for Her Beloved
section.sectionRationale: The bride voices a tender longing: that she might show her love openly, without shame, as freely as one would greet a brother in the street. She pictures leading her beloved home, resting in his embrace, and once more she charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love until the time is right. The short movement gathers up the Song's themes of open affection, secure rest, and love kept for its proper season.
section.thesis: The bride longs to love her beloved openly and without shame, rests secure in his embrace, and gives again the Song's refrain that love must not be stirred up until its proper time.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the bride's longing to show her love freely and to bring her beloved home; and the refrain of her rest in his embrace, sealed by the charge, do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.

units.label: A longing to love openly
units.note: as freely as one greets a brother

verses.text: O that you were to me like a {{ach|brother}} who nursed at my mother’s breasts! If I found you outdoors, I would kiss you, and no one would despise me.
I would lead you and bring you to the house of my mother who taught me. I would give you spiced wine to drink, the nectar of my pomegranates.

units.label: Rest in his embrace, and the charge
units.note: do not awaken love before its time

verses.text: His left hand is under my head, and his right arm embraces me.
O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you: Do not arouse or awaken {{ahavah|love}} until the time is right.

ach.gloss: Brother. The bride wishes her beloved were like a brother, not to lessen her love but so she could show it openly in public without reproach; the longing is for affection freely and honorably expressed.

ahavah.gloss: Love. The word that crowns the Song at 8:6. In the recurring charge, do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right, it names the powerful thing that must be honored and kept for its proper season rather than stirred up carelessly.

basic.context: The bride speaks a tender longing. In her world she could not show open affection to her beloved in public without reproach, but she could freely embrace a brother. So she wishes he were like a brother to her, only so that she could love him openly and lead him home to her mother's house without shame. She rests secure in his embrace, his left hand under her head, and then, for the third time in the Song, she charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up love until its proper time.
basic.hermeneutics: On the plain level this is a wife's longing for affection that can be shown openly and honorably, and her settled rest in her husband's love. The wish that he were like a brother is not about lessening desire but about being free to love without shame. Within the whole Bible, the longing to belong to the beloved openly, and the wisdom of keeping love for its right time, speak to the believer's longing for unhindered nearness to the Lord and to the patience love requires.
basic.originalLanguages: The bride wishes her beloved were like an ach, a brother, only so she could show her love in the open without reproach. She rests in his embrace, and then repeats the Song's refrain built on ahavah, love, the powerful thing that must not be awakened until the time is right, honored and kept for its proper season.
basic.typology: The longing to love the beloved openly and without shame foreshadows the day when the church will be with her Lord face to face, hidden love made open at last. The charge to keep love for its time pictures the patience of hope, the church waiting for the marriage of the Lamb.
basic.christ: The bride's wish, that she might belong to her beloved openly, unashamed before all, points to the day when the church will no longer love her Lord from afar but will be with Him face to face, the hidden made open. And her rest in his embrace pictures the security of those held by Christ, underneath the everlasting arms.
basic.god: God is not ashamed of His people, and He gives them a love in which they can rest secure, held and upheld. He also teaches His people patience, that love is powerful and good and must be honored in its proper time rather than seized carelessly.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 33:27, underneath are the everlasting arms. 1 John 3:2, when He appears we shall see Him as He is. Song of Solomon 2:7 and 3:5, the same charge not to awaken love before its time. 1 Corinthians 13:4, love is patient.
basic.oneStory: The bride longs to love her beloved openly and rests secure in his arms, charging that love be kept for its time. It pictures the believer's longing to be with the Lord unhindered, the security of being held by Him, and the patience of a love that waits for its proper season.

context.literary:
These four verses are the shortest unit in the Song, and they are almost entirely made of echoes. Verse 3 is word for word the line of Song 2:6, 'His left hand is under my head, and his right arm embraces me.' Verse 4 is the refrain of 2:7 and 3:5 with one clause removed: in the earlier two the daughters of Jerusalem are sworn 'by the gazelles and does of the field,' and here the oath formula is gone and only the plain charge is left. Verse 2 recalls 3:4, where she brought her beloved 'to my mother's house, to the chamber of the one who conceived me,' and the 'spiced wine' and 'pomegranates' recall the garden of chapter 4 and the invitation of 7:13.

The repetition is a structural device. The Song uses the embrace and the charge as a pair, a kind of seal on a section: 2:6-7 closes the first poem of springtime, 3:5 closes the night search, and 8:3-4 closes the long climb of chapters 5 to 8 before the final summit of 8:5 to 14. The reader who notices the pairing understands that each time the lovers are at rest, the poet pauses to teach the audience how to hold what has just been described.

The passage opens with a wish. The Hebrew idiom for 'O that' is a question, 'who will give,' the same construction Moses uses when he cries out for a people who might have the right heart, Deuteronomy 5:29. The first two verses are therefore not statements of fact but a speech in the subjunctive mood, picturing what she would do if there were no social obstacle. Verses 3 and 4 move from that wish into the actual present of her rest.

The wish is also placed carefully. It follows the climax of chapter 7, where she has invited him out to the vineyards, and it prepares the weightier final unit. After the lovers' union has been described, the poem steps back to say something about its public face.
context.historical:
The wish depends on the manners of the world in which the Song was written. In the family a brother was someone with whom a woman could be affectionate without scandal, and kisses between kin were ordinary. Jacob kisses Rachel at the well, Genesis 29:11, and Laban embraces and kisses Jacob, Genesis 29:13. Later, in the early church, believers greeted each other with a holy kiss, Romans 16:16. But a kiss given to a lover in the street was a different matter and could bring reproach, and Proverbs 7:13 shows the other side of this, where the adulteress seizes a young man in the street and kisses him in a shameless fashion. The bride's wish is for the freedom of family affection with the honour of marriage.

The word 'despise' also has a history. It is the same word used of Michal, who looked from a window and 'despised' David in her heart as he danced before the LORD, 2 Samuel 6:16. Public display of feeling could cost a person respect, and the poet knows it.

The 'house of my mother' is the household where a daughter is formed and where family arrangements are made. Rebekah runs to her mother's household to tell the news, Genesis 24:28, and Naomi sends her daughters-in-law back to their mothers' homes, Ruth 1:8. It was the women's side of the family, the place of welcome and instruction. Leading her beloved there is a way of bringing him into the family openly, without secrecy.

Spiced wine and the juice of pomegranates are among the luxuries of a well-provided house, and the offering of them is part of a bride's hospitality.
context.canonical:
The refrain of the charge is the Song's best-known line outside its own pages, and it has a wider echo in Ecclesiastes 3:5, which says there is 'a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing.' The Preacher and the Song agree that love, like every other good gift, has its season.

The longing to be near the beloved without hindrance finds its answers in the New Testament. Jesus promises that He will come back and take His followers to be where He is, John 14:2-3, and Paul says that after the Lord's coming 'we will always be with the Lord,' 1 Thessalonians 4:17. John writes that 'we will see Him as He is,' 1 John 3:2. The believer's present life, in Paul's words, is 'hidden with Christ in God' until Christ appears, Colossians 3:3-4, and that hiddenness is exactly what the bride of the Song wishes to end.

The security of verse 3 recalls Moses's blessing, 'underneath are the everlasting arms,' Deuteronomy 33:27, and the shepherd who carries lambs 'close to His heart,' Isaiah 40:11. The charge to wait is taken up by James: 'Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord's coming,' as the farmer waits for the rains, James 5:7-8. And Hebrews 2:11 gives the remarkable reversal of the wish in verse 1: Jesus is not ashamed to call His people brothers.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet teaches two things at once. First, love wants to be open. The bride is not ashamed of her beloved, and she wishes the world to see it. The words 'no one would despise me' say that her love is honourable and she longs for the freedom to show it. The poem treats secrecy as a burden to be borne until it can be lifted, and not as the proper condition of love.

Second, love wants to rest. The embrace of verse 3 is stillness. After the searches, the missed doors and the long ascents of the Song, it is notable that the poem pauses on a picture of being held. The poet means the audience to feel that love, at its best, is not only fire and pursuit but safety.

Third, he gives the charge for the third time. By repeating it, he means to fix it in the hearer's mind that love is not to be manufactured, rushed, or played with. It belongs to its time, and a wise person waits for that time. The first hearers, most likely young people in the family circle, would take it as the guide to the whole poem: what has been sung is good, and it is good because it is received at the right time and in the right place.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The wish of verses 1 and 2 is descriptive. It records a woman's feelings and a social situation, and it does not tell a church how it should regard public affection. Different societies draw the line in different places, and the Song does not set one for all. What it shows is that affection and honour should go together, and that a lover should not be ashamed.

The refrain of verse 4 is the nearest thing in the passage to an instruction, but it is spoken by the bride to the daughters of Jerusalem, not by God to the reader. Its force depends on what it says about love: that it has a proper time and ought not to be awakened carelessly. The wider Bible makes the application clear, since it places the fullness of physical love within marriage, Hebrews 13:4, and calls believers to self-control and to run from sexual immorality, 1 Corinthians 6:18. A reader who applies the charge to the single, the engaged, and the young is applying it in the sense the Song itself gives.

The passage should not be read as a ban on desire, and neither should it be read as permission to let desire run. It places love inside a larger order of wisdom, and it tells those who wait that they are not missing out but guarding something precious. For the married it counsels the same attentiveness: love should be kept from being treated as a toy.

debates.question: What exactly is the charge not to 'arouse or awaken love until the time is right'?

views.label: A warning against awakening sexual love before marriage
views.case: The most common reading takes 'love' as the whole passion of romantic and physical desire, and the charge as a counsel of patience to the unmarried. The Song's picture of covenant love supports this, since its fullest expression is in the marriage of 4:12 to 5:1. Hebrews 13:4 and 1 Corinthians 7 carry the same boundary.

views.label: A warning not to force love or interrupt it
views.case: Others point to the closing clause, literally 'until it pleases,' and take it as a statement that love comes of its own accord and cannot be conjured. On this view the daughters of Jerusalem are told not to disturb the lovers' rest, or not to hurry a person into feeling what has not yet grown.

views.label: Both, since love has an order and a season
views.case: A third view combines the two: because love rises when it will and cannot be commanded, it should not be provoked, and because it is powerful, it should be kept for the right place. This is how the verse is usually applied in teaching.

debates.bearing: The first and third readings are close in practice. The Song's own context treats desire as a fire, which verse 6 will say is fiercer than any other, and so it counsels care. The second reading adds that love cannot be forced, and that is also true.

debates.question: Why does she wish he were like a brother?

views.label: For the social freedom to show affection
views.case: The simplest answer is that kin could kiss in public without reproach, Genesis 29:11, while lovers could not. She wishes to have the same freedom without being despised.

views.label: To be openly acknowledged, rather than hidden
views.case: Others hear a deeper longing: she wants the relationship to be public and recognised, not conducted in secret. Leading him to her mother's house is the picture of that recognition, the family's welcome.

views.label: A sign the lovers are not yet married
views.case: Some think the wish makes sense only before marriage, since a wife would need no such pretext. The rest of the Song does not settle the question, and the wish may equally be the wistful thought of a wife who would like her love to be as visible as that of siblings.

debates.bearing: The text does not ask us to decide whether the lovers are formally wed at this point. Its lesson is the same under each reading: love is not something to be ashamed of, and a person may rightly long to see it honoured openly.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening words, 'O that you were,' translate a question idiom, mi yitten, literally 'who will give.' It is the same idiom Moses uses in Deuteronomy 5:29 when he longs for a people with the right heart. The bride's whole speech is therefore a longing placed in the form of a question: who will grant me this? It is the grammar of someone who knows that what she asks for is not in her hands.

The verb for kissing, nashaq, is the one from the very first line of the Song, 'Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth,' Song 1:2. The poem has come in a circle: it opened with a wish for the kiss, and it returns to the same wish after seven chapters, now with the added wish that the kiss be offered without any shadow of shame.

The verb in 'no one would despise me' is the verb buz, to hold in contempt. It appears again in verse 7, in the form that BSB renders 'utterly scorned,' where the man who offers all his wealth for love finds his offer treated with contempt. The same verb frames the two scenes. In verse 1 the bride fears contempt for loving openly, and in verse 7 contempt is what awaits anyone who thinks love can be bought. The word links the two ends of the passage, and perhaps of the whole chapter.

In verse 2 she says, 'I would lead you,' and the verb is nahag, the verb for leading a flock, as in Exodus 3:1, where Moses 'led the flock to the far side of the wilderness.' Without pressing it, the verb gives the sentence a gentle, pastoral sound: she would lead him as a shepherd leads, to her mother's home.

The verb for embracing in verse 3 is chavaq, the same word that Laban uses when he runs to meet Jacob and embraces him, Genesis 29:13. It is the ordinary word for a hug of welcome, and the word Ecclesiastes 3:5 uses for 'a time to embrace.' The Preacher's pairing of 'embrace' and 'refrain from embracing' is a useful commentary on the charge that follows.

The charge itself has two verbs, 'arouse' and 'awaken,' from two different roots, both meaning to stir someone from sleep. The oath word hishba'ti, 'I adjure,' is the verb of swearing, and in 2:7 and 3:5 it was followed by 'by the gazelles and does.' Here the oath formula is missing. The last clause, 'until the time is right,' is in Hebrew, literally, 'until it pleases,' from a root of delight and desire. The same root lies behind the name Hephzibah, 'My delight is in her,' which Isaiah 62:4 gives to the restored bride of the LORD. The thought is that love should come when it delights to come, not when it is summoned.

typology.type: The wish that he were like a brother, Song 8:1
typology.fulfillment: The bride wants the freedom of family love and yet to keep her beloved as her own. In Christ both are given. Hebrews 2:11-12 says that He who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are of the same family, 'so Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers,' and Romans 8:29 calls Him 'the firstborn among many brothers.' The church is both His family and His bride, a pair of images the Song never has to reconcile. The type falls short because the bride's wish concerns a human relationship still hindered by social custom, while Christ's open acknowledgment of His people is complete and without shame.

typology.type: Leading him to the house of her mother, Song 8:2
typology.fulfillment: The picture of being brought to the family home and welcomed finds its New Testament form in the Father's house. Jesus says, 'In My Father's house are many rooms,' and promises to return and welcome His followers, John 14:2-3. Paul calls the Jerusalem above 'our mother,' Galatians 4:26. The parable of the prodigal son shows the father who runs, embraces and kisses the returning son, Luke 15:20. The type falls short because the bride leads her beloved to a human household, while in the gospel the Lord is the one who goes ahead to prepare the place and leads His people home.

typology.type: His left hand under my head, his right arm about me, Song 8:3
typology.fulfillment: The embrace pictures the security of those who are held by God. Moses blesses Israel with 'underneath are the everlasting arms,' Deuteronomy 33:27, Isaiah 40:11 shows the shepherd carrying the lambs close to His heart, and Jesus says that no one can snatch His sheep from His hand, John 10:28. The type falls short because a human embrace ends, while the Lord's hold on His people does not.

typology.type: Do not awaken love until the time is right, Song 8:4
typology.fulfillment: The charge to wait corresponds to the church's patient hope. Paul says that we who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan inwardly as we wait for adoption, and that hope that is seen is no hope, Romans 8:23-25. James tells believers to be patient until the Lord's coming, James 5:7-8, and Titus 2:13 describes the church as awaiting 'the blessed hope.' Jesus tells a parable of ten virgins waiting for the bridegroom, Matthew 25:1-13. The type is a pattern and not a prediction: the Song's charge is about a human love, while the church's waiting is for a single Person, and the parallel should be held as a resemblance of posture.

study.christ:
The passage does not name Christ, and the plain reading is a bride's longing to love her husband openly and rest in his arms. The New Testament's teaching that marriage is a picture of Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31-32, gives the passage four lines to Him.

First, the wish of verse 1 is answered in a way the bride could not have asked. She wishes her beloved were her brother, that she might claim him without shame. In Christ the church has both: He is the bridegroom, and He is also the elder brother. Hebrews 2:11 says that He is 'not ashamed to call them brothers,' and Romans 8:29 says He is 'the firstborn among many brothers.' The shame the bride fears is borne in the gospel by the One who endured the cross, 'scorning its shame,' Hebrews 12:2. Where the Song's bride fears that the world will despise her love, Christ takes the world's contempt on Himself. Isaiah 53:3 says He was despised and rejected.

Second, the longing to be with the beloved openly is the church's present state. Believers love a Lord they have not seen, 1 Peter 1:8, and their life is 'hidden with Christ in God,' Colossians 3:3. The day when He appears, and 'we will see Him as He is,' 1 John 3:2, is the day when the hidden is made open. The bride's wish to meet him in the street and kiss him without reproach is a faint foreshadowing of that day.

Third, the embrace of verse 3 pictures what Christ already gives: security. The repeated line from 2:6 about the hand under the head says the bride rests in him, and Christ says, 'No one can snatch them out of My hand,' John 10:28. The Lord who is love holds His people as the Father holds the son He has run to meet, Luke 15:20.

Fourth, the charge that love be left until its time is the pattern of waiting in the Gospels. Jesus says that the bridegroom will be taken away and His friends will fast, but that He will return, Matthew 9:15. The church lives between the two, as the virgins waited with their lamps, Matthew 25:1-10. To wait is not to lose love. It is to keep the lamp trimmed.

As always, a caution is in order. Not every detail is a code, and the mother's house is not a prophecy of a particular church. The firm connection is that the bride longs for open union, rests in security, and waits for the right day, and so does the church.
study.god:
The passage shows God's character mostly by implication, through what a human love longs for and rests in, and by the way the Bible uses such pictures of Him.

First, God is not ashamed of His people. The Song's bride fears the world's contempt for her love, and the book of Hebrews says that Jesus 'is not ashamed to call them brothers,' Hebrews 2:11. The Lord acknowledges His own openly, in the assembly, and He does not make them wait in secret. For the believer who is despised for faith, this is a real comfort: the One who loves is not embarrassed by them.

Second, God is a place of rest. The embrace of verse 3 is stillness, not striving, and Scripture says the same of Him: 'The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms,' Deuteronomy 33:27. The same Psalm that says 'My soul clings to You' also says 'Your right hand upholds me,' Psalm 63:8, and in that verse the clinging and the upholding are held together. The God who is awesome and jealous is also the God in whose arms His people lie safe.

Third, God is patient and teaches patience. The charge of verse 4 reflects the order of a world in which good things have their season: there is 'a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing,' Ecclesiastes 3:5. The Lord of that order is not hurried. Peter says that He is patient with us, not wishing that any should perish, 2 Peter 3:9. And He asks His people to share that patience, 'Wait patiently for the LORD,' Psalm 27:14.

Fourth, God delights in His people and lets love rise at its time. The word behind 'until the time is right,' literally 'until it pleases,' is one of delight, and Isaiah 62:4 gives the name Hephzibah, My delight is in her, to the restored people. God's own love for His people is not forced from Him, since He is not moved by need. It is His pleasure, freely given, and the ancient promise says, 'I have loved you with an everlasting love,' Jeremiah 31:3.

Fifth, God honours the proper order of things He has made. The passage does not take the passion of love lightly, and the God who made it also fenced it with covenant, Hebrews 13:4. His holiness is not hostility to desire but care for what is precious.

For worship, the passage invites us to long for God with an open, unashamed desire, to rest in His hold, and to wait for His time. It is possible to praise God out of longing as much as out of fulfilment, and to say, with the Song's bride, that the best is still to come.

crossReferences.note: The first appearance of the embrace and the charge together. Verse 3 of our passage repeats 2:6 exactly, and verse 4 repeats 2:7 minus the oath by the gazelles and does. Reading them together shows that the pair works as a refrain meant to be remembered.

The bride brings her beloved to her mother's house and then repeats the charge. The sequence of finding, holding and bringing home is echoed in 8:2, which suggests she is still longing for the thing she once did, and now wishes she could do it openly.

The Song opens with a wish for kisses. In 8:1 the wish returns and is now joined to the wish for freedom from shame. The book has moved from desire to a desire that wants to be honourable and acknowledged.

Jacob kisses Rachel and Laban embraces and kisses Jacob. These are the family kisses that the bride has in mind in verse 1. They show that kisses and embraces between kin were an accepted and honourable part of ordinary life.

Michal looks down from a window and despises David in her heart for his open, joyful dancing. The verse shows what contempt for public display of feeling looked like, and it gives point to the bride's fear that someone would despise her.

There is a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing. This is the wisdom statement that stands behind the charge of verse 4: love has its season, and part of wisdom is to know which one it is.

The eternal God is a dwelling place, and underneath are everlasting arms. The bride's rest in her beloved's embrace is a human instance of the security that Moses sets before Israel as the lot of those whom God holds.
Jesus is not ashamed to call His people brothers. This is the gospel's answer to the wish of verse 1: the Lord openly owns those who are His and does not make them wait for acknowledgment.
Likeness to Him and sight of Him are promised for the day He appears. The longing for unhindered nearness, which the bride voices in verses 1 and 2, is fulfilled in this promise of sight.

The farmer waits for the rains, and believers are to be patient until the Lord's coming. It is the New Testament form of the charge to wait for the proper time, and it shows patience as strength of heart.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a love that had nothing to hide. The first man and woman were 'naked and unashamed,' and that single phrase of Genesis 2:25 is the pattern of what the Song's bride longs for in verse 1: to love without the fear of being despised. Genesis 3 then shows how shame entered. The first act of the fallen pair was to cover themselves and hide, and the history of the world since has been the long story of love that has to be hidden, and of shame that attaches to what was made good.

The Old Testament carries the longing forward. Israel's life is organised around a God who dwells in a tent and whose presence is veiled. The people cannot go in, and the nearness they have is mediated. Yet the prophets promise a day when the LORD will dwell with them openly and when they will be His people, and the Song's longing for unhindered nearness belongs to the same hope. The charge of verse 4, to keep love for its time, matches Israel's own long education in waiting, a waiting that the New Testament treats as a school for hope, Romans 8:23-25.

The story's turning point is Christ, who is not ashamed of His people and who bears the shame for them. He is the brother and the bridegroom, Hebrews 2:11, and in His resurrection the arms of the everlasting God are shown to have held. The church now lives in the time of the charge: she has the firstfruits and not yet the full harvest, the engagement and not yet the wedding. Her life is 'hidden with Christ in God,' Colossians 3:3, and her posture is the patient one that James urges, James 5:7-8.

The story ends in open love. John sees the bride made ready, Revelation 19:7, and hears that the dwelling of God is with man, Revelation 21:3. Nothing is hidden any longer and nothing is despised. 'We will see Him as He is,' 1 John 3:2, and the wish of Song 8:1, to love without shame and be received without contempt, is answered at last by the great welcome of the Father's house, John 14:2-3.

quiz.q: Why does the bride wish her beloved were like a brother in 8:1?

options.text: So she could show her love openly in public without reproach.
options.note: In her world a woman could freely greet a brother, but not a lover, in the street.

options.text: Because she no longer desires him as a husband.
options.note: Wishing him a brother might seem to cool her romance, but her desire is undimmed; she only longs to show it openly without shame.

options.text: Because she wants to be rid of him.
options.note: She longs to lead him home, not to be free of him.

options.text: Because family matters more than love to her.
options.note: She does reach for the image of a brother she could kiss in the street, but her wish is for open affection without reproach, not that family matters more to her than love.

quiz.q: How does the bride describe her rest in 8:3?

options.text: His left hand is under my head, and his right arm embraces me.
options.note: A picture of secure, tender rest in the beloved's embrace.

options.text: She stands alone, far from her beloved.
options.note: She is held close, resting in his arms.

options.text: She is anxious and cannot rest.
options.note: She is indeed with her beloved, but the picture is one of settled security in his arms, resting rather than anxious.

options.text: She holds him at arm's length.
options.note: His arms are truly in view, but his arm is around her in embrace, not holding her at arm's length.

quiz.q: What charge does the bride repeat to the daughters of Jerusalem in 8:4?

options.text: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.
options.note: The Song's recurring charge to honor love and keep it for its proper season.

options.text: Never allow yourselves to fall in love.
options.note: It rightly hears a call to restraint, but it overstates it; the charge honors love's right timing, it does not forbid love altogether.

options.text: Awaken love as quickly as you can.
options.note: The opposite: do not stir it up before its time.

options.text: Love is not worth the trouble.
options.note: The charge does counsel caution about awakening love too soon, but the Song prizes love as strong and good, to be kept for its season, not as something not worth the trouble.

quiz.q: How does the bride's longing to love openly point to the gospel?

options.text: It pictures the church's hope of being with her Lord face to face, love made open at last.
options.note: Now the church loves a Lord unseen; then she will be with Him openly, 1 John 3:2.

options.text: It teaches that love should always be hidden.
options.note: Her love is indeed constrained in public now, but the longing is precisely for love that can at last be shown openly, not for love that should always stay hidden.

options.text: It shows that God is ashamed of His people.
options.note: God owns His people openly; the longing reflects the hope of unhindered nearness.

options.text: It has nothing to do with Christ and the church.
options.note: It truly voices a human longing to love without reproach, yet the church has long heard here her hope of open, face to face love with her Lord, so it does point to the gospel.

questions: The bride longs to love her beloved openly, without shame. Where do you long for a day when your love for the Lord will be unhindered and complete?
His left hand is under my head. What would it mean for you to rest in the security of being held by Christ, underneath the everlasting arms, this week?
Three times the Song charges, do not awaken love before its time. Where is God calling you to patience, trusting His timing rather than seizing what is good before its season?
The bride pictured leading her beloved to the house where she was taught. Who taught you to love, and how might you honor that, or pass it on?
The bride was unashamed of her love. Are there ways you keep your devotion to Christ hidden that He may be calling you to bring into the open?

translationNotes.note: The wish that the beloved were like a brother reflects ancient social bounds: open affection to a brother drew no reproach, but to a lover it might; the longing is for love shown honorably in the open.
His left hand is under my head repeats the image of 2:6, a picture of secure rest in the beloved's embrace.
The charge, do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right, recurs at 2:7 and 3:5, honoring love and its proper season.
